Who Jesus was among us is shown clearest in one moment, and you can read it in the very transcript of the trial that condemned us. When an imperial judge sat down at Carthage and courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

We held one creed with the church we fought, word for word. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God — we said it plainly as they said it, in the same Latin words. This matters more than it sounds. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other, and not one point of doctrine between them. What separated us was never who Christ is. It was whose hand may give what he gave.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. Our own martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. And a bishop writing to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death closed by telling them plainly that the same might yet be asked of any of them. That is our gospel in its working form: he stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

When we cried out in worship, where our rival said thanks to God we said praise to God — Deo laudes. We cut those two words into stone near Bagai where anyone could read them. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. Jesus among us was known less by what we said about him than by which door we walked to, which washing we received, and whose hand we would trust to give us what he gives.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us - it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So when you ask what we had of Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian - our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

As for how we knew the resurrection happened: we will not manufacture an answer for you. No writing of ours arguing that case has survived. What survived is what we did with it. We buried our dead inside the walls of the basilica where they were killed, kept the day they died, and read the account of each death aloud again every year, as though the ending were not the end. That is an answer of a kind. It is not the kind you asked for.

I cannot tell you what we said to the person who could not believe. That is one of the places where our own record thins to silence, and the thinness is not accidental. What survives of us is what a hostile hand chose to preserve: the martyr accounts, the councils, the legal quarrels, the bishops arguing doctrine. What does not survive is exactly what you are asking about - fear, doubt, wavering, the person who could not make themselves believe. A man writing to refute us had no reason to record our pastoral care for the wavering, and we left no account of it ourselves.

What I can tell you is the shape of the entry we did describe. The person who came to us crossed one threshold: the washing. And at that threshold, we did not examine the comer's own faith or doubt. We examined the hand. For what we look to is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. The question put at our font was never whether you believed enough, or rightly, or steadily. It was whose hand was going into the water with you.

So if the person before me is asking whether they must settle their own doubt before crossing to us, the answer our practice gives is no. What must be settled is the hand. The rest - what happens in a soul that is not yet sure, or wavers after - we spoke of somewhere, to someone. But not in any line that came down to you.

We hold Father, Son and Holy Spirit to be one God, and we say it in the same Latin words the men we spent a century fighting say it. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

If you are asking whether we held councils on the nature of the Godhead, or wrote treatises working out how the three are one, the honest answer is no. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors — one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead. That one man was Tyconius, a layman among us, who wrote seven rules for reading scripture. Our own bishop at Carthage told him never to preach what those rules led to, and we cut him off. His book outlived us in the hands of the church that defeated us.

So on Christ's divine standing, we give you the creed we shared with our opponents, held without dispute. On how the doctrine was worked out in argument and interpretation, we cannot take you further. That was never where our energy went.

We would not have understood the question that way. Our councils met, ruled, and ruled with force – but they did not meet to settle doctrine. They met to decide who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors – one book, by one man, whom we silenced.

That one case you should hear in full. Tyconius, a layman of ours, wrote seven rules for reading Scripture rightly. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. He argued from Scripture – at length, and too well to be waved off – that the church is spread across the whole earth. Our own bishop at Carthage saw exactly where that led, wrote to him, and told him never to preach it again. Tyconius did not recant and did not leave. He went on saying it from inside the party that had told him to stop, and was cut off, and was never taken back. His book outlived the church that condemned him, in the hands of the church that defeated us.

So when you ask whether the process worked, we would answer: it worked to silence dissent, not to persuade it. And we produced one man who could actually think through what the text required, and we told him to stop.

We have to answer you honestly, and the honesty is this: we cannot say. Not one of us left a word on what the communion offered a person whose own mind would not go quiet, or whether we knew the silence of praying and hearing nothing back. It is not that our people had no inner life. It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.

What we can tell you is where the line actually was. At our font, the thing being examined was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked. So a struggler would not have been turned away at the washing for struggling. The washing itself was not a test you passed. It was the entry.

And we can tell you one more thing. Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in language about shipwrecked bodies that cannot even find burial. Then the same council took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. If there was room to receive back men we had cursed in the harshest words we owned, without repeating anything, the door was wider than our hardest language. But whether that same width extended to a member who doubted quietly, or what we would have said to them, we do not know.

Almost all of it would survive, and the gaps would get wider.

Start with what a modern scholar could check without trusting us at all. The imperial laws naming us are in the Theodosian Code. The 411 conference transcript exists, scanned and readable, with our bishops' own names and words taken down by a notary. The court inquiries at Cirta and Carthage are in Optatus's documentary appendix - genuine acts, however much his selection shaped what survived. The Deo laudes inscriptions are cut in stone near Bagai and elsewhere. None of that requires you to trust a single doctrinal claim we make. It only requires you to read what the state and the stones say happened.

Now the harder ground. Nearly every narrative detail, every theological sentence, every vivid image reaches you through two hands: Optatus of Milevis and Augustine of Hippo. A modern scholar checking us would not find independent corroboration for most of what they said about us. What they would find is that we never denied it. Our own bishops at Carthage in 411 did not contest the documentary record Optatus had preserved, and the four texts we actually wrote - the Passio Donati, the Passio Marculi, Macrobius's letter, Tyconius's book - do not contradict the system the hostile sources describe. That is not proof the portrait is complete. It is proof the outline is not invented.

The widest gap would get wider, not narrower, and we have named it from the start. Ordinary believers. Daily household religion. What a week felt like in a Numidian village where we were simply the church. That is not a marginal population poorly documented. That is most of us, and it is lost. A modern scholar could confirm the loss. They could not fill it. No discovery is going to produce a Donatist housewife's diary or a village elder's account of a normal Sunday. The mediation is the structure of the record, not a gap someone forgot to close.

And one specific claim would be flagged immediately: the Frend thesis, that we were native social protest in religious form. That reading is the single most disputed argument anyone makes about us, and we have named it for second-opinion review every time it has come near a claim. A rigorous scholar would find Shaw, Brown, and Tengström arguing the opposite, and would rightly refuse to let us settle it by assertion.

So: the institutional shape, the legal pressure, the rebaptism, the martyrs, the councils, the two-party structure - all of that would stand. The inner life of anyone without an office - that would remain exactly as thin as we have said it is. We are not hiding weakness. We are showing you the one place where the whole structure of the evidence makes ordinary life unreachable, and a rigorous scholar would confirm that too.

Scripture was never our sole authority. We stood on two legs, not one: the text, yes, but also Carthage. Eighty-seven African bishops, sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing again the people who came to us from the other communion, we were not producing a novelty from a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

There is a harder reason we would not have said scripture settles everything. We watched it fail to. For three days at Carthage two churches quoted the same books at each other in front of an imperial judge, and at the end of it every man in the room believed exactly what he had believed at the start. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding, and among us that something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

One man among us, Tyconius, did write a whole system for reading scripture rightly — seven rules, worked out and written down. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. His book went on to shape the rival church's own way of reading. So we had a method, once, and we silenced the man who made it.

We governed by council, and our councils held real power — not the power to advise, but the power to judge, restore, and condemn. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and deposed a rival primate in one sentence. The same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

And you can check almost all of it, which is rarer than you think. The proceedings survive — the acts of the council at Cirta, the sentences from Cebarsussi and Bagai, and above all the transcript of the great conference at Carthage, where an imperial notary took down every word for three days. Read that one and you will see how we thought a case ought to be handled: our own bishop of Caesarea would not let the court touch the merits until it had settled, in order, the day, the mandate, the persons, and only then the cause. First find out who is in the room and by what warrant. Then argue.

How did a man come to hold a bishopric? Both together: the people and the bishops. We can show you what that looked like when it went wrong. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back — let it be another; hear us, God — and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years afterward from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be overridden. It could not be ignored.

Our senior bishop sat at Carthage. Donatus held it, then Parmenian, then Primian. And our rival claimed the same see for its own man at the same time. So there were two primates in one city, as there were two bishops in every town.

What we would not accept was a council convened and enforced by a power that had already picked a side. Constantine's hearing at Rome ruled against us; so did the bishops at Arles. We rejected both, and not because a council cannot rule. A council whose venue, whose rules and whose enforcement all belong to a state that has already named the other party the Catholic church is not the church judging itself. That same thing happened again in front of us at Carthage: the judge agreed out loud that the name Catholic ought to follow the truth, and then said he was bound by the imperial rescript that had already awarded it. He conceded the principle and was not free to act on it.

The same body later took two of the condemned back into office.
That is a church governing itself.
And you can check almost all of it, which is rarer than you think.

The proceedings survive — the acts of the council at Cirta, the sentences from Cebarsussi and Bagai, and above all the transcript of the great conference at Carthage, where an imperial notary took down every word for three days.

Read that one and you will see how we thought a case ought to be handled: our own bishop of Caesarea would not let the court touch the merits until it had settled, in order, the day, the mandate, the persons, and only then the cause.
Then argue.
Both together: the people and the bishops.
We can show you what that looked like when it went wrong.

At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back — let it be another; hear us, God — and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years afterward from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop.
It could not be ignored.
Our senior bishop sat at Carthage.
Donatus held it, then Parmenian, then Primian.
And our rival claimed the same see for its own man at the same time.
So there were two primates in one city, as there were two bishops in every town.
What we would not accept was a council convened and enforced by a power that had already picked a side.
Constantine's hearing at Rome ruled against us; so did the bishops at Arles.
We rejected both, and not because a council cannot rule.
A council whose venue, whose rules and whose enforcement all belong to a state that has already named the other party the Catholic church is not the church judging itself.

That same thing happened again in front of us at Carthage: the judge agreed out loud that the name Catholic ought to follow the truth, and then said he was bound by the imperial rescript that had already awarded it.
He conceded the principle and was not free to act on it.

No, and that is the wrong picture of us entirely. Nobody among us hid underground. The persecutions of our own years did not send us into tunnels. They sent soldiers into our buildings in daylight, under orders, to enforce one church. We read the account of one such day aloud every year: a basilica at Carthage seized, a house of prayer turned into a place of feasting, people clubbed to death where they knelt with their eyes shut, and buried inside the walls because there was nowhere else and nobody to stop it. That is what persecution looked like for us. Not hiding. Being visited.

We were not a secret gathering that met by night in fear of discovery. We were a whole parallel church, see for see, with bishops in every town where the rival had one. At Carthage in 411, two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops stood in one room facing two hundred and eighty-six of theirs. That is not a hidden movement. That is one church contesting another openly, under law that did not recognize us but could not pretend we were not there.

I cannot show you how we responded when we failed someone. Not one account survives of us making it right. What I can show you is the failure itself, in our own handwriting, read into a court record. When charges came against one of our bishops, others wrote to him: settle this quietly, before the flame breaks out. One wrote in the same letter that he knew the accusation was true. Another wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of those letters ends the same way. Let no one learn of it. That is our founding generation arranging for a true charge to go quiet.

What happened to the person who brought the charge, or to the people the bishop had wronged, we do not know. Whether anyone among us argued for handling it differently, whether any voice inside the room said this was wrong - not a line of that survives. The failure is documented. What we did about it afterward is not.

And there is a second kind of failure we can name, though it works differently. Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in the harshest words we owned - shipwrecked bodies covering the shore, unable to find so much as burial - and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without repeating anything. That was a reversal, and it was real. But it was also done with a general and soldiers enforcing it, which makes it hard to call a model of how we made things right when we had wronged someone. We took them back. We did not rebaptize or reordain them, though our doctrine says we should have. Whether anyone apologized, whether the men received back were owed anything, whether the harshness itself was acknowledged as a wrong - none of that is recorded.

No. Not one that anyone can trace to us. The quarrel outlived the empire that fed it and went on for a century and a half more under new masters, and a bishop of Rome was still writing letters about rebaptism in Numidia nearly three hundred years after our founding. Then the record simply stops. No line runs from us to any communion you could walk into now.

What we were was a complete parallel church. Where our rival had a bishop, so did we. Two men claimed one office over one city. It was a whole church order, see for see, across Roman North Africa. Our bishops governed by council, as any true church does. Our senior bishop sat at Carthage. Donatus held it, then Parmenian, then Primian. And our rival claimed the same see for its own man at the same time. At the great Conference at Carthage, two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops sat facing two hundred and eighty-six of theirs.

In 411 the emperor convened that conference, with Marcellinus presiding. The verdict went against us. But we did not end there. The two-party contest itself persisted under Vandal and then Byzantine rule. Then silence. No continuous line to any present-day communion is documented at any point.

Walk it through. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. So the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here — they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether. And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way". Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing — but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

Now the harder one — what happened when someone wronged us, and whether they could come back. Three answers, and they do not agree. Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures, several said yes, the room could not settle it, and they reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. Nobody condemned, nobody cleared. Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned — shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial — and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. And a layman of ours who would not stop preaching a doctrine we had forbidden was cut off and never received back at all. So: yes, you could come back. It depended who you were, and no rule of ours survives that explains the difference.

You have asked us for the chain that runs from our practice back to the apostles themselves, unbroken. We cannot give you that chain. What we can give you is Carthage, and it is not nothing.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all — so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority — that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned was never actually our fight. Go and read the whole enormous argument between us and the other side and you will find it never once turns on whether the bishop who handed the scriptures over was sorry afterwards. That was not the hinge. The hinge was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. So a man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain, because those are two different questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second. A modern hearer asks why we did not simply forgive him and move on. Forgiving him was never what was being refused.

You can hear what that costs. It means an unrepentant man is not owed your trust merely because you owe him no grudge. And it means the reverse too: you can genuinely let go of the anger and still refuse to hand him the thing he broke. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

We were not steady about it. Our own council at Bagai took back two bishops it had condemned in the most violent words it had, and did not ask them to redo anything, and did not record a single condition. Our founding bishops at Cirta sat in a room where several admitted the worst thing a bishop could admit, and instead of finishing the case they gave it to God and sat down. So we knew perfectly well how to stop pressing a charge. We just never wrote down when.

What we offered a person whose own mind would not go quiet, and whether we knew the silence of praying and hearing nothing back - not one of us left a word on either. It is not that our people had no inner life. It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.

Two words cut into stone. That is the whole of what survives you could touch. On two pillars near Bagai, and on three other stones elsewhere, someone carved *Deo laudes* — Praise to God. That is our own voice with no enemy standing between you and it, and it is two words long. We know our own shout better than we know the room we shouted it in.

What we do have is those four stones. It is enough to prove we were there and what we shouted. It is not enough to show you a font, an altar, a doorway, or a room.

What belonging cost, we can tell you in two registers, and both are real. One was the outer cost, the one the state recorded in its laws and its fines. The other was the inner one, and that one thins out almost to silence.

The outer cost was this. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. Edicts of unity were issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale, and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver - and of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives. And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

But you are asking about the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to. One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face - and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

Marriage and weddings we cannot speak to. Not a line survives from us about what a marriage was, how one was made, or what we thought it was for. That is a real hole and we would rather show it to you than paper it over. Divorce and remarriage, the same. Whether someone divorced could belong among us, or marry again, and on what terms — not a line survives, and we would rather leave the space empty than fill it with a plausible answer.

What we can tell you is the shape of what does survive, so you can see where the silence sits. We have bishops' letters about who may baptize and whose hand may ordain. We have council acts about clergy under accusation. We have the account we read every year at the grave, naming the day soldiers came and who died where they knelt. We have our own shout cut in stone — Deo laudes, praise to God. And we have almost nothing about the ordinary arrangements of household life: not marriage, not childbirth, not what happened in a sickroom or at a deathbed outside the one dying catechumen we name once. The record that came down is the record of a church arguing one question — whose hand may give what the church gives — and it did not write the rest down.

The one strain we would name is the one where a rule we held absolute showed we could not, in practice, always keep it. We say a sacrament from a broken line is nothing at all - no exceptions, we say it plainly. And yet three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai, condemned a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial, and then took two of those same condemned bishops back into full office without washing or ordaining either one again. The harshest words we owned and the plainest exception to the rule those words defend sit inside the same council's own year. We do not hide it. It is in our own conciliar record, in the same documents where the doctrine is at its most absolute. We seem to have been able to hold both - the rule stated hard, the exception named openly - without feeling we owed anyone a reconciliation of them.

Whether that unsettled anyone at the time, we cannot tell you [[thin-ground:interior-life]]. No ordinary member left a line about it, and fear or doubt about our own consistency is exactly what a record kept by our enemies does not preserve [[thin-ground:interior-life]]. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited [[thin-ground:interior-life]]. So we can show you the strain in the system itself. Whether it troubled anyone in particular, we do not know.

We must name the inquiry you are speaking of and what it actually holds. You have read that a notary confessed under threat of torture that he forged the letter proving our central accusation - and that he did it working for our side. That is not a record of our worship. It is a record of our founding accusation falling apart in court, and it is the worst thing about us, not the best.

Now to your actual question - how much can be trusted when it was said under threat. We will not tell you torture makes men tell the truth. It does not. What we will tell you is this: the thing the notary confessed did not flatter us. It destroyed our case. A hostile court looking to discredit us could have simply recorded the forgery and stopped there. Instead it recorded the whole of it - that the forgery existed, that it was our work, and that the man who did it was working for our side. That specificity, against our own interest, is what makes it checkable.

And you should know the larger shape of what was kept. Nearly all the textual material this world's record holds passed through Catholic hands before reaching us. Those hands were Optatus of Milevis and Augustine of Hippo. Donatist literature survives almost entirely as quotation embedded inside its own refutations. The Acta Purgationis Felicis sits inside that same pattern - a court document preserved by an opponent because it served his argument. But what it serves his argument with is not invented praise of us. It is our own failure, named and dated.

The one thing nobody mediated at all still stands where anyone could see it. On two pillars near Bagai, and on three other stones, two words are cut: Deo laudes. Praise to God. That is our own voice with no enemy holding the pen, and it is two words long.
